bank.note: The separate financial, bench, and embankment etymologies converge on Germanic roots; the financial sense passed through Romance languages.

bark.note: The dog sound is Germanic, tree covering Norse, and the vessel name ultimately Egyptian through Greek and Romance.

ear.note: Both the hearing organ and a head of grain have Germanic roots.

lie.note: Both reclining and telling an untruth are inherited Germanic words.

rose.note: The flower is a Latin loan; the past tense of rise is Germanic.

spring.note: The season, water source, and verb spring are Germanic.

school.note: An educational school ultimately has Greek roots; a school of fish comes through Dutch.

tattoo.note: Body marking comes from Polynesian; the military signal comes from Dutch.

television.note: A mixed formation combining Greek tele- with Latin-derived vision.

die.note: Ceasing to live is Norse, the gaming/manufacturing noun Latin, and the obsolete spelling of dye Germanic.

pound.note: The unit of weight is a Latin loan; striking and an enclosure are Germanic.

inch.note: The measurement is a Latin loan; the Scots word for an island has Celtic roots.

furniture.note: Middle French fourniture derives from fournir, whose lexical root is Frankish; compare furnish.

trust.note: The current Wiktionary analysis favors a native Old English reflex; the traditional Old Norse derivation has a vowel-history problem.

wanna.note: A contraction of want (Norse roots) and to (native English).
